title: How the kingdom is remembered
hook: Sikhs remember it with pride and also discuss its failings

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Samadhi in Lahore, and your line was remembered in stone. Whose name did you read all the way through? Today, memory that isn't made of stone, and we close the week. Day nine hundred thirty-one.

A family dinner somewhere in the Punjab, or in Toronto, or in Birmingham. A grandfather is talking about Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the Lion of the Punjab, and the time when a Sikh flag flew over Lahore. His granddaughter has been reading too. She asks about the court's killings, the queens on the pyre, the ministers who sold each other out. For a moment the table goes quiet. Then the grandfather nods. Both of them are telling the truth. Today: how the kingdom is remembered.
screen: `A GRANDFATHER AND THE LION OF THE PUNJAB.` → `A GRANDDAUGHTER'S HARD QUESTIONS.` → `BOTH ARE TELLING THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: First, the pride. For many Sikhs, the kingdom of Ranjit Singh is a time when the Khalsa that had been hunted ruled in its own name. The Harmandir shone with gold. Coins carried the Gurus' names. A court of many faiths served one Maharaja, and mercy was part of his memory. Songs, paintings and family stories keep that alive. Second, the failings. Sikh writers and teachers also talk openly about what went wrong. The Maharaja was rebuked at the Akal Takht for his own conduct. His court was full of rivals. After his death, plots killed his heirs and ministers, and the army grew louder than the throne. And the queens and servants who died on his pyre are part of the story too. Third, why the Gurus make room for both. In a hymn of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, he says truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living. That sets a hard standard for remembering. A memory that only boasts isn't fully true. A memory that only blames isn't either. Fourth, the week. Look back at the road this week: the Maharaja's death, two heirs lost in a year, Sher Singh and the ministers, a child on the throne, the soldiers' councils, a samadhi of stone, and now this. It's been a hard week of the story. Holding pride and honesty at once is how a community keeps a kingdom without pretending about it. That's today's line.
screen: `THE PRIDE: THE KHALSA RULED.` · `THE FAILINGS, SAID OPENLY.` · `TRUTHFUL LIVING, HIGHER STILL.` · `A WEEK OF A HARD STORY.` · then, large: `PRIDE AND HONESTY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes holding both. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind something you belong to and care about: a family, a town, a team, a country, a community. First, let one thing you're proud of come forward. Rest with it for a few breaths. Then, gently, let one honest failing come forward too. Don't push the pride away to make room. Let them sit side by side, like two people at the same table. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
How the kingdom is remembered. With pride in what the Khalsa built, and honesty about what went wrong, both at the same table. Today's word.
screen: `HOW THE KINGDOM IS REMEMBERED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pride and honesty. Today, when you talk about something you love, name one thing it got wrong as well. Day nine hundred thirty-one.
